Passage:
When I first tried to master the art of balancing on my feet, I found myself clinging to the wall of the gym, fingers splayed and heart racing. Each attempt was a lesson in patience, a reminder that muscle memory could be coaxed into cooperation with enough repetition. After weeks of practicing on a soft mat, my body began to understand the rhythm of a handstand, and the awkward wobble turned into a steady, controlled upside‑down. It isn't difficult to do a handstand if you just stand on your hands.  

The next day, I boarded the orbital research vessel that orbited the Earth, expecting the usual hum of machinery and the sterile scent of clean air. Instead, a wave of savory aroma drifted through the airlock, and I realized it was the smell of seared steak, somehow carried from the station's galley to the observation deck. It caught him off guard that space smelled of seared steak.  

At a bustling networking event, a man tried to strike up a conversation with a woman who was clearly uninterested. He leaned in too close, offering a flippant joke, and she felt her discomfort rise. Without breaking eye contact, she began to gesture in the subtle, rhythmic language of her native sign system, conveying her boundaries clearly and confidently. When she didn’t like a guy who was trying to pick her up, she started using sign language.  

Looking back, I realize that the way we present ourselves is only one side of the story. The same gestures, words, or even silence can be interpreted in countless ways, depending on the observer's background and expectations. Each person who knows you has a different perception of who you are.
